hints: Think about what happens to the five d-orbitals when ligands approach a transition metal ion in an octahedral complex.
Consider what must happen to a d-electron for energy to be taken in from an external source.
Recall which region of the electromagnetic spectrum provides the right amount of energy for d-electron promotion.
Think about the link between the colour absorbed and the colour you actually observe when white light shines on the solution.
walkthrough:
Picture the d-orbitals splitting**
Start with the free $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ ion. Its five 3d orbitals all have the same energy. When six ligands approach octahedrally, they repel the d-electrons unequally. Two sets form, a lower set and a higher set with an energy gap, $\Delta$, that matches visible light energy. This is called d-orbital splitting.

Promote an electron across the gap**
$\text{Cr}^{3+}$ is $3\text{d}^3$, so there are electrons in the lower set that can move up. When the exact energy is supplied, one electron jumps to a vacant higher d-orbital. We say the electron is excited or promoted. No bonds are broken, it is purely a d to d transition.

Supply the energy from visible light**
That energy comes from absorbing a photon, $h\nu$, from white light. Only the wavelength whose photon energy equals $\Delta$ is absorbed. Different ligands change $\Delta$, so different complexes absorb different colours. That is why chromium complexes show so many colours.

See the colour left behind**
Your eye never sees the absorbed colour. It sees everything else. If red light is absorbed, blue-green light passes through and that is the colour observed. We call this the complementary colour, the transmitted or reflected light that is not absorbed.

Final answer: In an octahedral complex the d-orbitals split into two sets of different energy.
An electron is promoted from a lower energy d-orbital to a higher energy d-orbital.
Energy / a photon of visible light of a specific wavelength / frequency is absorbed to do this.
The colour seen is the complementary colour to that absorbed, the remaining wavelengths are transmitted / reflected.

hints: Use moles of $\text{AgCl}$ precipitated to decide how many $\text{Cl}^-$ ions are free counter ions and how many are bonded inside the complex.
Remember chromium(III) is six coordinate, so the total of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ plus $\text{Cl}$ inside the brackets must equal six.
Work out the charge on each complex ion by balancing $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ against the coordinated $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands.
Use the polar and non-polar data to decide which $\text{[CrCl}_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4\text{]}^+$ isomer is cis and which is trans.
walkthrough:
Separate free chloride from bound chloride**
Only ionic chloride outside the complex reacts with $\text{Ag}^+$ to give $\text{AgCl}$. Coordinated $\text{Cl}$ stays bonded to Cr and does not precipitate. So moles of $\text{AgCl}$ equals number of $\text{Cl}^-$ counter ions. For P, 3 mol $\text{AgCl}$ means all 3 Cl are free, complex is $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$. For Q, 2 mol means 1 Cl is coordinated, complex is $[\text{CrCl}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_5]^{2+}$. For R and S, 1 mol means 2 Cl are coordinated, complex is $[\text{CrCl}_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]^+$.

Check coordination number six**
Chromium(III) here is octahedral, coordination number 6. Count ligands inside: P has $6 \times \text{H}_2\text{O} = 6$. Q has $1 \times \text{Cl} + 5 \times \text{H}_2\text{O} = 6$. R and S have $2 \times \text{Cl} + 4 \times \text{H}_2\text{O} = 6$. That confirms your formulae fit the molecular formulae $\text{CrCl}_3(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6$, $\text{CrCl}_3(\text{H}_2\text{O})_5$ and $\text{CrCl}_3(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4$.

Draw octahedral 3D shapes**
Draw Cr in the centre with six bonds in octahedral arrangement. Use solid wedges for bonds coming out, hashed wedges for bonds going back, and normal lines for the plane. Place the correct ligands: all $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ for P, one $\text{Cl}$ for Q, two $\text{Cl}$ for R and S. Add the correct overall charge outside square brackets.

Assign cis and trans using polarity**
R and S have the same formula but different polarity, so they are cis-trans isomers. In cis-$[\text{CrCl}_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]^+$, the two $\text{Cl}$ are at 90 degrees, adjacent, giving an unsymmetrical polar ion. This is R. In trans, the two $\text{Cl}$ are at 180 degrees, opposite each other, giving a symmetrical non-polar ion. This is S.

Final answer: P: $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$ octahedral, 3 $\text{Cl}^-$ outside.
Q: $[\text{CrCl}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_5]^{2+}$ octahedral, 2 $\text{Cl}^-$ outside.
R: cis-$[\text{CrCl}_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]^+$ octahedral, 1 $\text{Cl}^-$ outside.
S: trans-$[\text{CrCl}_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]^+$ octahedral, 1 $\text{Cl}^-$ outside.
All drawn octahedral with 3D wedge / hashed bonds, correct formulae and charges, R with adjacent Cl, S with opposite Cl.

hints: Focus on the trans arrangement in S and think about the directions of the two Cr-Cl bond dipoles.
walkthrough:
See why opposite bonds cancel**
In trans-$[\text{CrCl}_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]^+$, the two polar $\text{Cr-Cl}$ bonds point in exactly opposite directions at 180 degrees. Their dipole moments are equal and opposite, so they cancel. The $\text{Cr-O}$ dipoles also cancel in pairs, leaving no net dipole, so S is non-polar.
Final answer: In S the bond dipoles cancel due to symmetry, the trans Cl ligands are opposite each other.

hints: Recall what the term dentate tells you about the number of bonding sites on one ligand.
Think about what a ligand must donate to the central metal ion to form each coordinate bond.
walkthrough:
Define bidentate precisely**
Bi means two. A bidentate ligand uses two atoms on the same ligand molecule to bond to one metal centre. Each bonding atom donates one lone pair into a vacant orbital on the $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ ion, forming two coordinate bonds. Picolinate does this through its N atom and its carboxylate O atom.
Final answer: A species that donates two lone pairs to a metal atom / ion, forming two coordinate / dative bonds.

hints: Compare picolinic acid, with $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, to its anion and decide which proton is lost.
walkthrough:
Remove the acidic proton**
Picolinic acid is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_4\text{N-CO}_2\text{H}$. The carboxylic acid proton is acidic, the pyridine ring is not. Deprotonation gives the picolinate anion, $\text{C}_5\text{H}_4\text{N-CO}_2^-$. Draw the same pyridine ring with N at the bottom and a $-\text{CO}_2^-$ group attached to the carbon next to N, showing the negative charge on the carboxylate.
Final answer: Pyridine ring with $\text{CO}_2^-$ substituent at the 2-position, N unchanged.

hints: Multiply the number of ligands by the denticity to find the total number of coordinate bonds to Cr.
walkthrough:
Count bonds from three bidentates**
Three picolinate ions each form 2 bonds, so total bonds $= 3 \times 2 = 6$. Coordination number is therefore six. Six coordinate chromium(III) is octahedral. The $3+$ charge on Cr is exactly balanced by three $1-$ picolinate ligands, giving the neutral complex $\text{[Cr(picolinate)}_3\text{]}$.
Final answer: Coordination number six and geometry octahedral around Cr.

hints: Assign usual oxidation numbers $+1$ for H, $-2$ for O and $+1$ for $\text{NH}_4^+$ as a group, then solve for Cr.
walkthrough:
Solve for Cr in each compound**
In $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$, each $\text{NH}_4^+$ is $+1$, so $2 \times (+1) + 2x + 7 \times (-2) = 0$. This gives $2x = +12$, so $x = +6$. In $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3$, $2x + 3 \times (-2) = 0$, so $2x = +6$ and $x = +3$. Chromium is reduced from +6 to +3.
Final answer: $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$: Cr is +6; $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3$: Cr is +3.

hints: Identify the products as $\text{N}_2$, $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, then balance N and H to find the water coefficient.
walkthrough:
Balance the volcano reaction**
The inert colourless gas from ammonium dichromate is nitrogen, $\text{N}_2$. Write the skeleton: $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 \rightarrow \text{N}_2 + \text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. N balances with 1 $\text{N}_2$, Cr balances with 1 $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3$. H needs $8$ H on the right, so $4\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Check O: $7$ on left, $3 + 4 = 7$ on right. The balanced equation is $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 \rightarrow \text{N}_2 + \text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
